Surah al-Jinn (The Jinn)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said, 'Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, which guides to righteousness, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.'"﴾

In it is the affirmation that the jinn listened to the Qur'an, were amazed by it, were guided by its guidance, and believed in God. The indication of this has already been given in the words of the Shaykh, may God's mercy be upon us and upon him, in Surah al-Ahqaf, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] when We directed to you a company of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. The verse of al-Ahqaf also explains what that company of the jinn did after hearing the Qur'an: when their listening was completed, they returned to their people as warners.

In it is also an explanation that they had knowledge of the Book of Musa, which is the Tawrat (Torah), and they testified that the Qur'an confirms what was before it, and that it guides to the straight path, as is stated here in His saying: ﴿It guides to righteousness﴾.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 72, verse 4:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that our foolish one used to speak about Allah an extreme transgression﴾

Al-shatat (extreme deviation) means a distance that is excessive in its remoteness. ʿAntara said in his mu'allaqa (the celebrated ode of pre-Islamic poetry):

؎Far has become the place of visiting for lovers, so that the daughter of Makhram has become difficult for those who seek her.

It is also narrated as:

؎She has alighted in the land of the visitors, and so has become...

He also recited for someone else:

؎The place of visiting at Jadhwa has grown distant, and hope has come to an end.

In both verses, *al-shatat* means excessive distance. In the first he says, "she has become difficult for her seekers," and in the second, "hope has come to an end." The Qur'an has made clear that *al-shatat* here means a specific distance, namely distance from the truth, as in His saying: ﴿So judge between us with truth and do not exceed justice﴾ [Sad: 22]. (p-318)

It also includes distance from the reality of monotheism toward polytheism, which is what is meant here, as in the surah "al-Kahf" in His saying: ﴿We would never invoke besides Him any deity; we would have certainly spoken then an extreme transgression﴾ [al-Kahf: 14], because their invoking other than Allah is the furthest thing from the truth.

What indicates that this is the meaning here is what comes in this same surah: ﴿So we believed in Him and will never associate with our Lord anyone﴾ [72:2

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 72, verse 8:

Allah's statement: ﴿And we touched the heaven and found it filled with a strong guard and meteors﴾

Allah, the Exalted, explained the purpose of that guarding: it is to protect the heaven from eavesdropping (istiraq al-sam', stealing hearing). This is as in His statement: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of stars﴾ ﴿and as protection﴾ [al-Saffat: 6-7]. Allah, the Exalted, also explained their condition before that, namely that they used to sit in positions from it for listening, so they would steal a word and descend with it to the soothsayer (kahin), and he would lie with it a hundred lies. Allah, the Exalted, also explained that the meteors come to them from the stars.

As in His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5].

The Quranic verse, "And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance," is a text showing that the jinn do not know the unseen. Allah the Exalted has stated this clearly in His words: ﴿So when We decreed death for him, nothing showed them his death except a creature of the earth eating away at his staff. Then when he fell, the jinn realized that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment.﴾ [Saba': 14].

There may appear to be a problem with this verse, since they first said: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an, guiding to right conduct, so we have believed in it﴾ [al-Jinn: 1-2], and then they say: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾ [al-Jinn: 10]. The reality is that they wondered when they touched the sky and were prevented from it because of its intense guarding. Then they acknowledged at last when they heard the Qur'an and learned the reason for the strengthening of the sky's guard, because when they were prevented, what came to their minds was that it was for the sake of revelation. This is supported by His words: ﴿And that they thought as you thought, that Allah would never resurrect anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 7].

His words, the Exalted: ﴿And that we touched the sky and found it filled with strong guards and meteors﴾ [al-Jinn: 8], indicate by implication that they were prevented from listening, as they said: ﴿Whoever listens now will find a meteor lying in wait for him﴾ [al-Jinn: 9]. (p-319) However, one might suppose that they would still attempt to listen even with the intense guarding, but Allah the Exalted has stated clearly that they did not and will not listen after that, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, they are removed from hearing﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 212].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 72, verse 15:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

Surah al-Jinn (The Jinn)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And as for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾

It does not contradict His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42]

Because al-qasit (the deviator, the unjust) is the one who oppresses, and al-muqsit (the just, the equitable) is the one who acts justly, so the two are opposites.

All of these are texts indicating that when the community keeps to the upright way, the divine law (shari'ah), God opens up to them blessings from heaven and earth.

Similar to this is His saying: {I said: Ask your Lord for forgiveness; indeed He is ever Forgiving. He will send down abundant rain upon you from the sky, and aid you with wealth and sons, and make for you gardens and make for you rivers} [Nuh: 10-12].

The implication of this is that whoever does not keep to the way, his deviation or his polytheism may be the cause of his being deprived of God's blessing upon him, as is stated explicitly in His saying: {Set forth for them the parable of two men: for one of them We had made two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them tilled land. Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth within them, and he had abundant fruit} [Al-Kahf: 32-34].

He had no band to help him against God, nor was he one who could help himself} [Al-Kahf: 34-43].

How closely the present resembles the past, in what the Muslim world is living through today between the two opposing tendencies, the communist and the capitalist. That is the sunnah of God in His creation. As for His saying {that We may test them therein} [Al-Jinn: 17], meaning: We try them regarding what they do of thanking for the blessing and spending it on what pleases God, or of transgressing with it and withholding its due right? So fear God as much as you are able} [At-Taghabun: 15-16].

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 72, verse 18 (part 1 of 7):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone along with Allah﴾.

"Al-masājid" is the plural of "masjid." Linguistically, "masjid" is a noun of place on the pattern *maf'il*, like *majlis* (sitting place), which is irregular in form. Linguistically, it applies to every place suitable for prostration (sujūd).

The Sunnah has established that the whole earth is suitable for this, as in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration (masjid) and a means of purification (ṭahūr)." He excluded from this certain places in which he forbade prayer, because of attributes that apply to them. These are: the place where refuse is dumped (*al-mazbalah*), the slaughterhouse (*al-majzarah*), the graveyard (*al-maqbarah*), the middle of the road (*qāri'at al-ṭarīq*), the top of the bathhouse (*fawqa al-ḥammām*), places of ground subsidence (*mawāḍi' al-khasf*), camel resting places (*ma'āṭin al-ibil*), the usurped place (*al-makān al-maghṣūb*), on which there is a difference of opinion regarding the validity of prayer there or its invalidity, and churches (*al-biya'*).

Our Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, counted nineteen places when commenting on Allah's words: ﴿And the companions of al-Ḥijr denied the messengers﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 80], in his discussion of the ruling on the land of al-Ḥijr and the places of subsidence. He cited the evidence for each place. It is a lengthy, comprehensive discussion.

In customary usage (*'urf*), the masjid is whatever is designated for prayer. This is the meaning intended here by the annexation (*iḍāfah*) to Allah, the Exalted. It is an annexation of honour and dignity, with an indication that it is specific to Allah, meaning reserved for His worship and remembrance, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; glorifying Him therein in the mornings and the evenings﴾ ﴿Men whom neither commerce nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah and establishing prayer﴾ [al-Nūr: 36–37].

For this reason, it is forbidden to use them for worldly matters such as selling and trade, as in the ḥadīth: "If you see someone selling or buying in the masjid, say to him: 'May Allah not make your trade profitable.'" Narrated by al-Nasā'ī, and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan.

Likewise, announcing a lost item (*inshād al-ḍālla*), because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "If you hear someone announcing a lost item in the masjid, say to him: 'May Allah not return it to you, for the masājid were not built for that.'" Narrated by Muslim.

In the ḥadīth of the Bedouin who urinated in the masjid, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "These masājid were not built for this; they are only for the remembrance of Allah and what is related to it." In the *Muwaṭṭa'* of Mālik, it is related that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) built an open area (*raḥbah*) on the side of the masjid called al-Baṭḥā'. He said: "Whoever wishes to make noise (*yalghaṭ*), or recite poetry, or raise his voice, let him go out to this open area."

*Al-laghaṭ* is speech that involves clamour and confusion.

Regarding *al-* in *al-masājid*: it is for *istighrāq* (comprehensiveness), meaning it indicates the inclusion of all masājid, just as it indicates equality in its generality. However, verses came that single out some masājid for additional merit and distinction. These are:

**Al-Masjid al-Ḥarām.** Allah the Exalted singled it out by what He mentioned in His words: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾ ﴿In it are clear signs; the station of Ibrāhīm; and whoever enters it is safe. And for Allah, from the people, is a pilgrimage to the House﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 96–97]. Here He mentioned seven characteristics that are not shared by other masājid: that it is the first House established for mankind; that it is blessed; that it is a guidance for the worlds; that in it are clear signs; the station of Ibrāhīm; that whoever enters it is safe; and that ḥajj and ʿumrah are directed to it, along with other signs.

**Al-Masjid al-Aqṣā.** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām to al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ [al-Isrā': 1]. It was singled out by being the place of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) night journey (*maṣrā*) to it, by the blessing around it, and by the Prophet (ﷺ) being shown among its signs of his Lord.

It would have been possible for him to ascend to the heavens from the heart of Makkah, from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām. However, it was so that He might show him some of Allah's signs, like road markers, so that they would be evidence for him against Quraysh when he informed them of the night journey and the ascension (*al-isrā' wa'l-mi'rāj*). Also, Jibrīl presented him with three cups: water, milk, and wine. He chose the milk as a symbol of *al-fiṭrah* (natural disposition). Also, the prophets gathered for him and he prayed with them in al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, whereas he had seen them in the seven heavens. All of this was among the signs of Allah, which He showed him (ﷺ) in al-Masjid al-Aqṣā.

**Al-Masjid al-Nabawī and Masjid Qubā'.** As for Masjid Qubā', the verse about it was revealed: ﴿Surely a masjid founded upon piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108].

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim it came that Abū Sa'īd asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which masjid was founded upon piety from the first day?" He (ﷺ) took a handful of pebbles, struck them on the ground of his masjid, and said: "It is this masjid of yours."

In *Bulūgh al-Marām* and elsewhere, there is the ḥadīth of Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with him): that "the Prophet (ﷺ) asked the people of Qubā', and he said: 'Indeed Allah praises you.' They said: 'We follow up the stones with water.'" Narrated by al-Bazzār with a weak chain (*sanad ḍa'īf*).

Ibn Ḥajar said: Ibn Khuzaymah graded it ṣaḥīḥ from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) without mention of the stones.

The author of *Wafā' al-Wafā'* said: Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated through several chains, the gist of which is that when the verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to the people of Qubā'.

In another narration: "the people of that masjid."

In another narration: "the Banū 'Amr ibn 'Awf." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has praised you well regarding purification. What is your purification?" They said: "We cleanse ourselves with water."

He said: Aḥmad and Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated, and the wording is Aḥmad's, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "I set out to Masjid al-Taqwā, along with 'Abdullāh ibn 'Umar and Samurah ibn Jundub, and we came to the Prophet (ﷺ). They said to us: 'Go to Masjid al-Taqwā,' so we set out towards it. His hands met the shoulders of Abū Bakr and 'Umar, and we were startled in his presence. He said: 'Who are these, O Abū Bakr?' He said: 'ʿAbdullāh ibn 'Umar, Abū Hurayrah, and Jundub.'"

The ḥadīth of Muslim concerns the masjid of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and those texts concern Masjid Qubā'.

Ibn Ḥajar, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The truth is that each of them was founded upon piety." His words: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108] are clearly about the people of Qubā'.

It has been said that the ḥadīth of Muslim, concerning specifically the masjid of the Prophet (ﷺ), came in response to a disagreement between two men about which masjid the verse referred to. So the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to make clear to them that the verse is not specific to Masjid Qubā', but is general to every masjid founded upon piety. The lesson is in the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause (*sabab*), as is well known in the principles of jurisprudence (*uṣūl*).

Accordingly, the verse includes, and does include, every masjid wherever it may be, provided its foundation from the first day of its construction was upon piety. The context of the verse, relative to what comes before and after it, supports this. Before it came the story of the Masjid of Harm (*Masjid al-Ḍirār*), with Allah's words: ﴿And those who took a masjid for harm and disbelief, and to cause division among the believers, and as a station for whoever had warred against Allah and His Messenger previously. And they will surely swear, "We intended only good." And Allah testifies that they are liars﴾ ﴿Do not stand in it ever. A masjid founded upon piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107–108].

It is well known that the Masjid of Harm was in the area of Qubā', and they asked the Messenger (ﷺ) to pray for them in it, outwardly seeking blessing, but in reality to establish its existence, using that as a pretext. However, Allah exposed their reality.

The verse came with a comparison between the two masājid. Allah said to him: ﴿Do not stand in it ever. A masjid founded upon piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it, in it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ and so on [al-Tawbah: 108].

Immediately after that, there came a second comparison, more general than the first, in His words: ﴿Is he who founded his building upon fear of Allah and His pleasure better, or he who founded his building upon the edge of a crumbling cliff, so it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ ﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts﴾ [al-Tawbah: 109–110].

Thus, the cause of the revelation of the verse is the comparison between two differing principles. The priority (*awwaliyyah*) in the verse, in His words: ﴿from the first day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108], is a relative priority, meaning relative to every masjid at the first day of its construction. Although the apparent meaning is a specific temporal priority, namely the first day the Prophet (ﷺ) reached Madīnah and stayed at Qubā', this comparison in the verse remains in effect until whatever time Allah wills, in every time and place, as we have stated.

These four masājid are distinguished by matters that link them together by many ties. The most important of these is that the determination of their location was by revelation or something similar to revelation. Regarding the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Ḥarām), there is His words: ﴿And when We settled for Ibrāhīm the place of the House﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 26].

Regarding al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, there is what came in a report from him: that Allah revealed to His prophet Dāwūd: "Build Me a house." He said: "Where do You want me to build it for You, O Lord?" He said: "Where you see the knight standing, brandishing his sword." So he saw it in its present place, and it was an enclosure belonging to a man from the Children of Israel. Up to the end of the story in al-Bayhaqī.

Regarding Masjid Qubā', there is a report with a weak chain: "When he (ﷺ) arrived at Qubā', he said: 'Who will mount the she-camel?'" until 'Alī mounted it. He said to him: "Loosen her reins," and she bolted. He said: "Mark out the masjid where she bolted."

Regarding al-Masjid al-Nabawī, it came in all the biographies (*siyar*) that: "Whenever he passed by one of the quarters of Madīnah, and they said to him: 'Come to the wealth and the equipment,' he would say: 'Let her go on her way, for she is commanded.' Until she reached in front of the house of Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī (may Allah be pleased with him). In front of it was a drying yard for orphans and a Jewish graveyard. He bought the place, dug up the graves, and built the masjid."

Likewise regarding the construction: all of them were built by the messengers of Allah. Al-Masjid al-Ḥarām was built by Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), meaning the building which the Qur'an mentioned. There are many reports concerning what preceded it, but what is established in the Qur'an is His words: ﴿And when Ibrāhīm was raising the foundations of the House, and Ismā'īl﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127].

Likewise, Bayt al-Maqdis: between it and the (Sacred) House there were forty years, as in the ḥadīth of 'Ā'ishah in al-Bukhārī. That is, the renewal of its construction.

Likewise Masjid Qubā': the Prophet (ﷺ) took part in its construction. In the account of its construction, a man met the Prophet (ﷺ) carrying a stone, and said: "Let me carry it for you, O Messenger of Allah." He said to him: "Go and take another, for you are no more in need of the reward than I am."

Likewise his noble masjid in the illuminated city of Madīnah, when he first built it from palm trunks and palm fronds, and then rebuilt it again with construction after his return from Tabūk.

Because of these particularities of these four masājid, they were distinguished from the general masājid, as we have stated.

Among the most important of these is the multiplication of the reward for deeds performed in them, the root of which is prayer. Al-Bukhārī indicated this by his chapter heading: "Chapter on the virtue of prayer in the masjid of Makkah and Madīnah." He cited two ḥadīths.

The first is the ḥadīth: "Do not undertake journeys (*lā tushaddu al-riḥāl*) except to three masājid: al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, and the masjid of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

The second ḥadīth is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A prayer in this masjid of mine is better than a thousand prayers in any other, except al-Masjid al-Ḥarām."

Also, al-Masjid al-Nabawī is singled out by its *rawḍah* (garden), which is one of the gardens of Paradise.

By his (ﷺ) saying: "My pulpit is upon a canal (*tarʿah*) of the canals of Paradise," and this is a famous ḥadīth: "Between my house and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, and my pulpit is upon a canal of the canals of Paradise."

Masjid Qubā' is singled out by his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever purifies himself in his house, then comes to Masjid Qubā' and prays two rak'ahs in it, will have the reward of an ʿumrah." Ibn Mājah and ʿUmar ibn Shabbah narrated it with a good chain, and Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim narrated it, and al-Ḥākim said: ṣaḥīḥ with a chain.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 72, verse 18 (part 2 of 7):

He said in Wafa' al-Wafa': 'Umar ibn Shabbah said: Suwayd ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Ayyub ibn Hayyam related to us, from Sa'id ibn al-Ruqaysh al-Asadi, who said: Anas ibn Malik came to us at the Mosque of Quba', and he prayed two rak'ahs near some of these pillars. Then he gave the salam and sat, and we sat around him. He said: "Glory be to Allah! How great is the right of this mosque. Even if it were a month's journey away, it would be deserving of being visited. Whoever leaves his house intending it, relying upon it, to pray four rak'ahs in it, Allah will return him with the reward of an 'umrah."

This meaning became well known among the common people and the elite, to the extent that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hakam said in a poem of his:

؎ If I die, then I have certainly gladdened an eye with the women who perform 'umrah to Quba',
؎ Those whose necks are slender and soft, upon whom is the beauty of radiance and splendour.

Ibn Shabbah related, with a sound chain, through the route of 'A'ishah bint Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: I heard my father say: "To pray two rak'ahs in the Mosque of Quba' is dearer to me than to come to Bayt al-Maqdis twice. If people knew what is in Quba', they would ride camels' livers to it (i.e., travel hard to it)." And other narrations, both attributed to the Prophet and to companions, that affirm this meaning: that Quba' is singled out in that whoever performs purification in his house, comes to it intending it, and prays two rak'ahs in it, he has the reward of an 'umrah.
