Note.

Here a question imposes itself: why was the Mosque of Quba' singled out above others, and why was purification required in one's house rather than near the mosque? I have searched for this at length and did not find a statement on it. Then it appeared to me, from the reality of its history and its connection to the reality of the Muslims and the Masjid al-Haram, that the Mosque of Quba' has many connections with the Masjid al-Haram:

First: in terms of time, it is older than the Mosque of Madinah.
And in terms of relative precedence: the Masjid al-Haram is the first house set for mankind.
And the Mosque of Quba' is the first mosque built by the Muslims.
The Masjid al-Haram was built by the Friend (al-Khalil, Ibrahim).
And the Mosque of Quba' was built by the Seal of the Messengers.
The site of the Masjid al-Haram was chosen by Allah, and the site of the Mosque of Quba' is similar to it.
And in terms of purpose: the Masjid al-Haram is a sanctuary and refuge for the one who stays and the one who comes from the desert.
And the Mosque of Quba' is a sanctuary, dwelling and refuge for the early emigrants and the people of Quba', so praying in it has a strong connection with the Masjid al-Haram, making the one who purifies in his house and intends to it to pray there like one who has the reward of an 'umrah. If it is said that requiring purification in one's house, not near the mosque, is a sign of great care for it first, and a sifting of intention toward it second, and an approximation to the act of requiring ihram for 'umrah from the outside of the sanctuary (al-hill), not from near the House, in the actual 'umrah, since it is far: then purifying from one's house and going to Quba' to pray in it is like entering ihram from the hill and entering the Haram for the tawaf and sa'i. Also in it is compensation to the emigrants for what they missed of neighbouring the Sacred House before the Conquest. And Allah knows best.

* *

Another note.

Among what should be known: the mosque in Islamic society has a great mission, which Muslims are most obliged to revive: that the mosque is for them the house of the community among them, for all their general and particular interests, approximately to the extent of what suits it. The Prophet's Mosque in the earliest period of the Muslims was thus the model for this.

For it was the place of prayer whose prayer is multiplied, and it was the institute for receiving knowledge from him ﷺ, and from Jibril (peace be upon him), and from the imams, the heirs of the prophets. It still remains so, praise be to Allah, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The time is near when people will ride camels' livers seeking knowledge and will not find a scholar like the scholar of Madinah."

And as he said: "Whoever goes to my mosque to learn knowledge or to teach it is like one who fights in the way of Allah." There was in it the teaching of children to read and write, and it still is so until today, praise be to Allah. It was a seat for issuing fatwas, a place of judgment, a place of hospitality, a dwelling for prisoners, and a clinic for the wounded.

A dome was pitched for Sa'd in it when an arrow struck him, so that the Prophet ﷺ might visit him from nearby. It was a headquarters for command, where battle banners were tied, peace treaties concluded, and a lodging for delegations, such as the delegations of Tamim and 'Abd al-Qays; and a treasury for money, such as the arrival of the wealth of Bahrain and the guarding of it by Abu Hurayrah.

When the treasury of the Muslims was broken into, 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to his agent there: "Move it to the mosque, for the mosque remains a place of prayer in it," i.e., so that he may take charge of guarding it, and as a resting place for the unmarried and a lodging for strangers. And other such things that are not found in any other institution, and which can only be realized in the mosque, which confirms the mission of the mosque and calls for attention to it and good benefit from it.

* *

On the occasion of these four mosques being singled out for greater virtue and increased multiplication of prayer, there are several topics in the Prophet's Mosque in particular that have often been referred to in several places, and they are of great importance. The most important of them are four topics, which we present briefly:

The first: the multiplication of prayer by a thousand. Is this specific to his ﷺ mosque which was built by his ﷺ construction, or does it include what was added to it of extensions?

Likewise the extension of the rows outside it beyond the crowding; is it only for obligatory prayer or does it include voluntary prayer too? Is it for men and women, or for men only?

(p-328) And the matter of the forty prayers, the second after the first expansion by 'Umar and 'Uthman, and the moving of the mihrab to the qiblah from the Rawdah. Which of the two rows is better: the first row or the rows of the Rawdah?

The third: the prayer of the followers in front of the imam at times of crowding.

The fourth: the hadith of travelling (shadd al-rihal) and greeting upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Then there comes a topic that necessitates connecting the beginning of the verse with its end: "And that the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone along with Allah" (72:18),

because of what it contains of alluding to and indicating the building of mosques over graves, along with sincerifying worship to Allah alone.

These topics I had explained in detail in my treatise on the Prophet's Mosque which I wrote earlier, and we summarise them here.

The first topic.

Is the excellence specific to obligatory prayer, or to voluntary prayer? The majority agreed on obligatory prayer, and disagreement occurred regarding voluntary prayer, except for the greeting-of-the-mosque two rak'ahs after Friday prayer and two rak'ahs before Maghrib.

As for the disagreement regarding the regular sunnah prayers in the five daily prayers and in qiyam al-layl, the cause of the disagreement is the generality of: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere." Whoever takes it in its generality includes voluntary prayer, and whoever restricts the generality to its original basis confines it to obligatory prayer, since a general term in absolute form is understood in terms of what is more specific, which is the obligatory prayer.

The hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit appears in Abu Dawud and others: "The best prayer of a man is in his house, except the prescribed prayer."

And there came explicit mention of his mosque in the words: "A man's prayer in his house is better than his prayer in this mosque of mine, except the prescribed prayer."

And what came from al-Tirmidhi in al-Shama'il and Majma' al-Zawa'id: that 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about praying in one's house and praying in the mosque, and he ﷺ said: "You see how close my house is to the mosque; so for me to pray in my house is dearer to me than to pray in the mosque, except the prescribed prayer."

And in another narration: "Do you see the nearness of my house to the mosque?" He said: Yes. He said: "Indeed I pray the voluntary prayer in my house."

* *

The second topic.

The opinions of the imams (may Allah have mercy on them). In accordance with this detail, the opinions of the imams (may Allah have mercy on them) were as follows:

The opinion of Imam Abu Hanifah: voluntary prayer in the house is better, and if it is performed in the Prophet's Mosque it has the same reward, i.e., it is general in all prayers. But it is better in the house than in the mosque.

According to al-Shafi'i: the narration from him differed. Al-Nawawi in his commentary on Muslim mentioned the generality. There came from him in al-Majmu' what indicates the specificity, though he did not state it explicitly.

The texts concerning voluntary prayer in the house are numerous, among them: "Make your prayers in your houses."

And among them: "Honour your houses with some of your prayers."

Al-Qurtubi mentioned from Muslim: "When one of you finishes the prayer in his mosque, let him set aside for his house a share of his prayer."

According to the Malikis: it covers both obligatory and voluntary prayer, and they argued for that by saying that the hadith is in the context of favour, and an indefinite noun in the context of favour is general, i.e., his saying ﷺ: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere," where "prayer" is an indefinite noun.

And in the context of favour and bestowal of this great reward, it is general for obligatory and voluntary prayer. What appears, and Allah knows best, is that there is no disagreement between the two groups, since the excellence of a thousand is obtained for every prayer a person prays in it, whether obligatory or voluntary.

Praying voluntary prayer in the house is better than in the mosque, due to his ﷺ constant practice of voluntary prayers in the house despite his house being near the mosque. Likewise this excellence includes the prayer of a man and of a woman.

(p-330) But the prayer of a woman, nevertheless, is better in her house than in the mosque. This is the second topic, i.e., which of them is better for a woman: praying in her house or in the Prophet's Mosque?

This question was examined by our honoured Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him) at the words of the Exalted: "In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; therein glorify Him in the mornings and the evenings, men..." (24:36–37).

And that the concept of "men" is a concept of attribute in this matter, not a concept of title. Accordingly, women glorify Allah in their houses. He pursued the research thoroughly regarding the generality of mosques and the specificity of the Prophet's Mosque, which is sufficient for elaboration.

* *

The third topic.

It is: is the multiplication specific to his ﷺ mosque which he built, and which existed during his ﷺ lifetime, or does it apply to it and to what was added to it after him?

The point of the discussion is what came in the text of the hadith: the demonstrative "in this mosque of mine." Some scholars said: the demonstrative is established for specification. The scholars of linguistic theory said: it is established by a general concept for a specific referent, so in use it is restricted to a particular individual, namely what was suitable for sensory indication, and this is precisely what existed at the time of the Prophet ﷺ.

It is known that the indication did not encompass the extension that came after that indication, and from here the disagreement and questioning arose.

This question arose in the time of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) at the first extension he made to the Prophet's Mosque. He saw some of the Companions avoiding prayer in that extension and preferring the old part of it. So he said to them: "Had I not heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wish for the expansion of the mosque, I would not have expanded it." And by Allah, it is truly the mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ even if it extended to Dhu al-Hulayfah, or even if it extended to San'a'. This is the point and cause of the discussion.

But if it is said that in the same hadith there is another linguistic topic, namely that his ﷺ saying "in my mosque," with the attribution to him ﷺ, and attribution indicates specification or definiteness.

And it has the meaning of generality and comprehensiveness, and now, with the extension at every time and over the passing of days, it has still remained the mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and upon this was 'Umar's declaration: "Indeed it is the mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

Opinions of the scholars: the majority hold that the multiplication applies to all its parts, including the extension. It is reported from al-Nawawi in his commentary on Muslim that it is specific to the mosque (as it stood at the time).

The first (view): before the extension. It was said that he retracted it. This retraction is found in al-Majmu' Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, and upon this there remains no disagreement on the matter.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 72, verse 18 (part 3 of 7):

Ibn Farhun said: I came across a statement of Malik, who was asked about this, and he said: "I do not think that he (peace be upon him) indicated by his saying, 'in this mosque of mine,' anything except what would come to be a mosque after it, and that Allah had informed him of that."

I have already pointed out that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) did not enlarge the mosque except after he had heard from the Messenger (ﷺ) his desire for the enlargement, so this serves as confirmation of the view of Malik (may Allah have mercy on him). It is also narrated: "He (ﷺ) said one day while he was in his prayer place in the mosque: 'If only we were to enlarge our mosque,' and he pointed with his hand towards the qiblah." 

In another narration: "I intend to extend the qiblah side of our mosque," which indicates that the enlargement was in the mind of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Despite the desire for the enlargement, there came no indication of anything that would change the ruling of prayer in that expected enlargement. It cannot be said that before it existed no ruling could attach to it, because we have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) establish rulings concerning matters that did not yet exist, such as the stations for ihram (mawaqit al-ihram) of the Egyptians, the Syrians and the Iraqis, and his saying (ﷺ): "Yemen will be conquered, Syria will be conquered, Iraq will be conquered," and with each of them he said: "There will come a people who drive (their people) saying, 'Come to ease and plenty,' so they will carry off their families and whoever obeys them, while Madinah is better for them, if only they knew."

Some said: his saying (ﷺ), "in this mosque of mine," is to exclude the assumption that the other mosques attributed to him in Madinah are included, other than this mosque, not to exclude what would be added to the Prophet's Mosque. This was said by al-Samhudi. End of quotation.

But it is not known that there were several mosques belonging to him (ﷺ); there was only the mosque and the musalla (prayer ground), and the remaining mosques were given that name by convention.

Ibn Taymiyyah has a concise statement on this, which is that the enlargement took place in the times of ʿUmar and ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with them both). The enlargement by each of them was on the side of the qiblah. Nevertheless, each of them, when he led the people in prayer, stood in the qiblah area located in that enlargement. It is therefore impossible that prayer in that enlargement should lack the merit of the mosque, for that would entail the prayer of ʿUmar and ʿUthman leading the people being without merit.

Praying with the people in the first rows in a less excellent place, while leaving the more excellent one, is (also to be considered). End of quotation.

From all that we have presented, it becomes clear that the ruling on the enlargement of the Prophet's Mosque is like the ruling on the original mosque regarding the multiplication of reward up to a thousand (fold).

I had heard from our Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him) what indicates this, and this will come, Allah willing, in the section on the forty prayers, and on the prayer of people in the row outside the mosque.

Note: The scholars unanimously agreed that this multiplication is in quality, not in quantity. So if a person owed the missed prayers of one day, five prayers, and he prayed one prayer which is better than a thousand prayers, it would not discharge any of those missed prayers from him. In my view, it is like two garments, one of which is worth a thousand dirhams and the other one dirham. Each of them is a garment for its purpose, and no more than one person can wear it at one time, however high its price.

Likewise (it is like) a pen and a pen: however expensive the pen, two persons will not write with it at the same time.

Another note: Undoubtedly the original mosque has features that do not exist in the rest of the mosque, such as the Rawdah (the Garden) of Paradise, and the minbar standing over one of the channels of Paradise, and some of the pillars with their history.

Al-Nawawi said: If the person is going to pray alone or a supererogatory prayer, the better is that he be in the Rawdah, and otherwise in the first mosque (the original). If he is in congregation, he must seek out the first row, and otherwise (he may pray) in any place in the mosque. This has a rational basis. Praise be to Allah.

* *

The Fourth Question.

After this expansion and the moving of the first row away from the Rawdah, is it better to pray in congregation in the first row, or in the Rawdah while being behind the first row? To illustrate this question, we present the following:

In front of the musalla there are two places:
One of them is the Rawdah, whose merit is that it is a garden from the gardens of Paradise.
And the first row, concerning which it is said: "If they knew what the first row is, they would draw lots for it." So which of the two places takes precedence over the other?

It is known that before the enlargement, they could combine the two virtues, since the first row was in the Rawdah.

But now, after the expansion, the first row has separated from the Rawdah, as long as the imam prays at the front of the mosque. I have not come across a detailed treatment of this question.

However, there are general statements from al-Nawawi and Ibn Taymiyyah, as we have presented in the section on whether the multiplication extends to the enlargement. There is also a case from which the answer can be inferred. Before the expansion, the first row had a right side and a left side, and the right side had merit over the left. It is known that the right side of the row before the expansion lay to the west of the minbar, that is, outside the Rawdah, while the entire left side was in the Rawdah. Nevertheless, they preferred the right side over the left side for its own sake, and the Rawdah also (was preferred) for its own sake. So if the right side, which was outside the Rawdah, was given precedence by them over the Rawdah, then the first row is to be given precedence all the more.

There is also a legal truth mentioned by al-Nawawi, namely giving precedence to the essential attribute over the accidental attribute. Here, the first row is an essential attribute of the congregation, while the merit of the Rawdah is an accidental attribute of the place. That is, for every state, whether remembrance, an obligatory prayer or a supererogatory prayer, giving precedence to the first row, because it is essential to the congregation, is more appropriate than giving precedence to the Rawdah, because it is accidental.

(p. 334)

Al-Nawawi illustrated this principle by saying: If a person on his way to pray at the Prophet's Mosque found another mosque where a congregation was praying, and he had to choose between joining the congregation with these people or leaving it and going on to the Prophet's Mosque, and thereby missing the prayer, so that he would pray alone (at the Prophet's Mosque) for a thousand prayers' reward, he said: it is better for him to pray in this mosque in congregation, because attaining the congregation is an essential attribute of prayer, while attaining (the reward of) a thousand prayers is an accidental attribute due to the merit of the Prophet's Mosque. End of quotation, summarized.

It may also be said: the servant is charged with performing the prayer in congregation more than he is charged with performing it in the Prophet's Mosque.

Such is the situation: we are required to (seek) the first row absolutely, wherever it is, more than we are required to pray in the Rawdah. And Allah knows best.

* *

The Fifth Question.

This concerns the situation where the mosque is crowded and the rows extend outside into the street or the open courtyard. Is there, for the extension of the rows, that multiplication of reward or not?

Let us know that the merit of congregational prayer is established without disagreement. As for the multiplication up to a thousand, I have not come across a text on it. I asked our Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him) about this twice. In the first instance, he inclined to the view that it is restricted to the mosque. In the second instance, about ten years later, he inclined to the view that the reward is general, and he said something to the effect that the increase is a bounty from Allah, and this is a grace upon His servants. So what is hoped for, in the vastness of Allah's bounty, is that there will not be two men in the row side by side, one of them on the threshold of the mosque facing outward and the other on it facing inward, with this one receiving a thousand and that one receiving one. Their shoulders are pressed together, and this is clear. Praise be to Allah.

I have seen in the matter of Friday prayer among the Malikis a text, and likewise among others who make the mosque a condition for Friday prayer, for they agree that when the rows extend onto the streets and the open spaces outside the mosque, the Friday prayer is valid, even though they held it outside the mosque. But since the rows extended from the mosque to outside it, the ruling of the mosque applied to them and the Friday prayer was valid.

So we say here: likewise, since the rows are outside the Prophet's Mosque, the ruling of the mosque will extend to them, Allah willing. And Allah knows best.

(p. 335)

This may be supported by custom: if you asked someone who prayed in such a situation, "Where did you pray? In Quba'? Or in the Prophet's Mosque?", he would say: "No, in the Prophet's Mosque." Thus he has not, by custom, gone outside the designation of "mosque."

* *

The Sixth Question.

This concerns crowding specifically in the Prophet's Mosque, and generally in the rest of the mosques, when the place becomes cramped and the worshippers are compelled to pray in many rows outside the mosque, while being ahead of the imam by several rows. What is the ruling on the prayer of these people?

Al-Nawawi, in al-Majmu', mentioned the disagreement from al-Shafiʿi, and that the correct position in the school is validity with disapproval (karahah).

The Malikis also mentioned validity, and they cited as evidence for it the prayer of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) one night at the house of Maymunah (may Allah be pleased with her), with the Prophet (ﷺ) praying.

Ibn ʿAbbas was then a youth. He stood on the left of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed him on his right, honouring the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When (the Prophet) became aware of him, after he had said the takbir and entered into the prayer, he (ﷺ) took him by the hand and moved him from behind, and placed him on his right, level with him, in the position of a single person, as is known from the ruling on one praying alone with the imam.

The point of the evidence in this is that the directions relative to the imam are four: behind him, which is for the many, two or more; on his right, which is the position of the single person; and his left and his front. As for the left, Ibn ʿAbbas stood there, and it is not a position (for standing), so (the Prophet) took him and placed him on his right.

However, after he had entered the prayer and had performed some of his prayer in that position (on the left), his prayer was valid, since he built upon the part he had earlier performed on the left, because of the necessity of his ignorance of the position.

As for the front of the imam, it is not a position for standing. But in case of necessity and because of crowding, it was unavoidable to be ahead of the imam, so it was permitted, or it was valid, because of necessity, just as it was valid on the left of the Prophet (ﷺ). And Allah knows best.

This evidence is strengthened by the following: if a person came to the congregation and found no place for himself except beside the imam (p. 336), he would stand on the imam's right beside him, just as if he were praying alone, even though there were many rows. But his standing was valid because of necessity.

* *

The Seventh Question.

The topic of the forty prayers. It is in one respect specific to the Prophet's Mosque, and in another respect general to every mosque, but not as forty prayers, rather as forty days. As for what pertains to the Prophet's Mosque, it has come in the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever prays in my mosque forty prayers, without missing a prayer, will have written for him an acquittal and deliverance from punishment, and he will be cleared of hypocrisy."

al-Mundhiri said in al-Targhib wa'l-Tarhib: its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih. Ahmad recorded it in his Musnad, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat.

In Majma' al-Zawa'id: its men are trustworthy (thiqat). It is in al-Tirmidhi with the wording: "Whoever prays forty days in congregation, catching the first takbir, will have written for him two acquittals: an acquittal from the Fire and an acquittal from hypocrisy."

al-Tirmidhi said: it is mawquf (stopping at a companion) upon Anas, and I know of no one who raised it (to the Prophet).

Mulla ʿAli al-Qari said: "Something like this is not said by opinion," and some people have criticised this hadith on two grounds:
As for the first: because of Nubayt ibn ʿUmar.
As for the second: from the aspect of its being raised or stopped. Some scholars who examined these two hadiths carefully regarding the chain confirmed the soundness of the first, and ruled that the second is to be treated as raised. Shaykh Hammad al-Ansari devoted a treatise to both of them, in which he refuted some of the later scholars who criticised them. We summarise his statement in what follows:

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 72, verse 18 (part 4 of 7):

The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in Ta'jil al-Manfa'a fi Zawa'id al-Arba'a: Nubayt ibn Umar. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat (the Trustworthy Narrators), and so there was agreement on the authentication (tawthiq) of Nubayt by Ibn Hibban, al-Mundhiri, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Hajar, and none of the imams of this discipline criticised him. Therefore it is not permissible for anyone to impugn, or to declare weak, one whom reliable imams have authenticated, and no imam of the discipline of criticism (jarh) and authentication (ta'dil) has opposed them. And the imams of this discipline whom they mentioned suffice as exemplars.

That is so. Even if it is assumed, for the sake of argument, that there is some objection regarding the chain, the imams of hadith do not prohibit acting upon it when the hadith contains no halal or haram ruling and no matter of belief, but rather concerns the chapter of virtues of deeds (fada'il al-a'mal). They do not forbid acting upon it, because the chapter of virtues is not subjected to this degree of strictness.

al-Suyuti transmitted something similar from Ahmad and Ibn al-Mubarak.

As for the hadith about attaining the takbir al-ihram in any mosque, this is more general than the subject of the Prophet's Mosque that we are discussing, and all its chains are weak. However, the Hafiz Ibn Hajar said: it falls within what is acted upon in the chapter of virtues of deeds. End of the summary.

As for this exhortation to forty prayers in the Prophet's Mosque, it is perhaps, and Allah the Exalted knows best, of the kind of familiarisation and provision (al-ta'awwud wa'l-tazawwud), because of what that deed brings of persistence and eagerness to perform the five prayers in congregation for eight days, and of the person's constant preoccupation with the matter of prayer and his eagerness for it, so that no prayer escapes him, and his heart becomes attached to the mosque. The congregation becomes for him a habit (malakah), and he becomes at ease in frequenting the mosque, eager for the remaining prayers during the rest of his days, so that the congregation does not escape him except through an excuse.

If he was a visitor and returned to his country, he returns with this commendable quality. Perhaps the multiplication of the prayer by a thousand is like a concentrated, very potent medicine, of quick benefit, more than what came in general mosques with forty days in which the takbir al-ihram is not missed. For forty prayers in the Prophet's Mosque equal forty thousand prayers elsewhere, and they equal roughly the prayers of twenty-two years.

And if we consider the reward of congregation, twenty-five degrees, it would equal the prayer of one praying alone for five hundred and fifty years, that is, in reward and recompense and not in number, that is, qualitatively and not quantitatively, as we have previously stated. And Allah's bounty is great.

Let it be known that the purpose of these forty prayers is, as we have previously stated, familiarisation and eagerness for congregation.

As for one who returns and abandons congregation and is careless about the matter of prayer, we seek refuge in Allah, this would be the utmost relapse. We ask Allah for well-being. And we know that these forty prayers have no connection either with the Hajj or with the visit, as was previously set out for the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, in the etiquette of visitation in the surah "al-Hujurat".

And the visitation is completed by praying two rak'ahs of the greeting of the mosque, and greeting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his two companions, may Allah's good pleasure be upon us and upon them, then supplicating for oneself and for the Muslims with good, then, if he wishes, he departs to his family, and if he wishes, he sits for as long as is convenient for him. And success is from Allah the Exalted.

* *

Section on greeting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

It has previously been set out by the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, an aspect of the aspects of greeting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when speaking on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lest your deeds be rendered void while you perceive not﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], in warning against things that nullify deeds, and clarifying what is a right of Allah that must not be directed to other than Him, and what is a right of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that must not be exceeded.

The discussion of greeting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his merit and his excellence may lead to the subject of journeying (shadd al-rihal) to the mosque, and to greeting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

* *

Journeying to the Prophet's Mosque for greeting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Among what is specific to the Prophet's Mosque, indeed among its most important distinctions after the prayer, is the greeting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from within this mosque, in the past and in the present.

As has come in the Sahih: "There is no one who greets me except that Allah returns my soul to me, so that I return his greeting" (ﷺ). And they are agreed that this occurs for one who greets him (ﷺ) from nearby, and this greeting never occurred on any day except from the Prophet's Mosque, whether before or after the room (hujrah) was incorporated into the mosque.

It is well known that the first of the etiquettes of visitation and of greeting him (ﷺ) is beginning with the prayer of two rak'ahs of the greeting of the mosque, and after the greeting he turns away from facing (the grave), and supplicates as he wishes, wherever he is in the mosque.

Here is a question over which dispute has long been raised: journeying (shadd al-rihal) for the greeting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Although its proper place is the discussion of visitation and its rulings and etiquettes, we shall present a brief account of it on the occasion of the hadith on journeying, and we ask Allah the Exalted for guidance and success.

It is known that the origin of this question is the hadith: "The saddles are not to be tightened (for travel) except to three mosques", mentioned previously; due to their disagreement over the estimation of what is excluded from it. The meaning of journeying to it (in those mosques), is it specifically for the prayer, or for the prayer and other than it?

To grasp the reality of this question, we should first know that the discussion of this question has three situations:

First: journeying to the Prophet's Mosque for visitation. This is agreed upon.

Second: visiting the Messenger (ﷺ) and greeting him from nearby without journeying, and this too is agreed upon.

Third: journeying for visitation only. This third situation is the locus of the discussion among them, and the subject of the earlier debate.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari on the hadith of journeying: al-Kirmani said: many debates occurred on this question in our age in the Syrian lands, and disputes were written on it from both sides.

I say: that is, Ibn Hajar says: it refers to what Shaykh Taqi al-Din al-Subki and others replied with against Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah, and what al-Hafiz Shams al-Din Ibn Abd al-Hadi and others defended for Ibn Taymiyyah, and these are well known in our lands. End quote. This gives us the extent of the disagreement on it and its history.

Ibn Hajar indicated the summary of the view on it by his saying: The majority permitted by consensus journeying for visiting the Prophet (ﷺ), and that the hadith "The saddles are not to be tightened" is only intended as specifically the prayer, and there is no place more worthy of prayer for which saddles are tightened except the three mosques, because of the excellence of the multiplication of prayer in them.

Taqi al-Din made the subject of the prohibition on journeying general to prayer and to other than it. It was objected to him with the consensus of the Ummah on the permissibility of journeying to any place, for several reasons, as is well known.

Among what has been cited as evidence for not journeying merely for visitation is what was narrated from Malik: the dislike of saying: "I visited the grave of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

It was answered concerning this: Malik's dislike was of the wording only, out of courtesy, not that he disliked the act of visitation itself, for it is among the best deeds and the most exalted acts of drawing near that lead to the Lord of Majesty, and its legislation is a matter of consensus without dispute. And Allah is the Guide to what is right. End quote.

Perhaps the school of al-Bukhari, judging by his arrangement, is the school of the majority, because in the same chapter, directly after the hadith of journeying, he brought the hadith: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere", which suggests that he intended to show that the reason for journeying is the excellence of prayer, so the prohibition of journeying is specific to the mosques, and for the sake of prayer, except to those three mosques, because they are singled out for the multiplication of prayer in them over the rest of the mosques and other places.

Ibn Hajar discussed the wording of the hadith and preferred this view, saying:

Some of the verifiers said: his saying "except to three mosques" has an elided excluded term. It may be estimated as general, so that it becomes: the saddles are not to be tightened to a place for any matter except to the three. Or it may be estimated more specifically. There is no way to the first, since it would lead to closing the door of travel for trade, maintaining kinship ties, seeking knowledge and other things, so the second is determined.

And the better: that what is more fitting be estimated, namely: the saddles are not to be tightened to a mosque for prayer in it except to the three. Thereby the saying of one who prohibits journeying to visit his noble grave, peace and blessings be upon him, and the graves of the righteous, is invalidated. And Allah knows best.

Al-Subki the Elder said: there is no spot on earth that is preferred in itself so that saddles are tightened to it except the three lands. By excellence I mean what the Shari'ah has recognised and on which it has built a legal ruling. As for other lands, saddles are not tightened to them for their own sake, but for a visit, or jihad, or knowledge, or the like of recommended or permissible matters.

He said: this has been confused for some of them, who claimed that journeying for visitation to one who is in other than the three is included in the prohibition, and this is an error, because the exception is only from the genus of the excluded term. So the meaning of the hadith is: the saddles are not to be tightened to a mosque among the mosques, or to a place among places, for the sake of that place itself, except to the three mentioned. Journeying for visitation or for seeking is not to the place, but to the one who is in that place. And Allah knows best. End quote.

By reflecting on the words of Ibn Hajar, we find that it contains an equation applied to the text of the hadith, that it has only two situations:

First: it is said: the saddles are not to be tightened except to the three mosques for the specific purpose of prayer, and they are not to be tightened to other places for the sake of prayer. Thus the prohibition is directed at tightening saddles to any place other than the three mosques for the sake of praying in other than them. Non-prayer then remains outside the prohibition, so saddles may be tightened to any place for it.

Non-prayer includes: seeking knowledge, trade, recreation, contemplation, jihad and the like, and the texts on all of this are abundant.

As for seeking knowledge, there are the texts we have mentioned previously, and the Prophet of Allah Musa journeyed to al-Khidr, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Musa said to his young man, "I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas or continue for a long period."﴾, up to His saying: ﴿"Indeed, we have suffered from this journey of ours, fatigue."﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Musa said to him, "May I follow you on condition that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?"﴾ [al-Kahf: 60-66].

As for travel for trade, there is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. And His saying: ﴿It is He who made the earth docile for you, so walk in its broad paths and eat of His provision﴾ [al-Mulk: 15], and others are numerous.

As for travel for contemplation, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe"﴾ [al-Naml: 69].

And His saying: ﴿Then We destroyed the others. And indeed, you pass by them in the morning, and by night. Then will you not reason?﴾ [al-Saffat: 136-138].

And His saying: ﴿And how many a city have We destroyed while it was wrongdoing, so it is now fallen upon its trellises, and abandoned wells and lofty palaces. Have they not travelled through the earth so that they would have hearts by which to reason or ears by which to hear? For indeed, it is not eyes that are blind, but blind are the hearts within the breasts.﴾ [al-Hajj: 45-46].

Allah has commanded His servants to travel, so that they may reason with their hearts concerning the condition of those desolate towns, and be admonished by the circumstances of their people.

(p. 342) These are the texts permitting travel for several purposes, and among them is travel to visit the Prophet ﷺ and to greet him with peace. Greeting the Prophet ﷺ is among the acts prescribed in the Law without dispute. The second case is that the prohibition is general to all places and all purposes, so that the saddles are never to be fastened except to the three mosques and their three cities. However, this is not limited to prayer alone, but applies to everything that is prescribed in its origin, of the kinds we have already mentioned: seeking knowledge, trade, admonition, recreation, and other things, such as fasting, i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque), settling in a place for worship (mujawarah), Hajj, 'Umrah, maintaining ties of kinship, and viewing historical landmarks, and the like.

From all of this comes the greeting of peace upon the Messenger of God ﷺ. So if one sets out for Madinah for any purpose that includes visiting and greeting the Messenger of God ﷺ, there is no objection in either case, and the mentioned hadith does not conflict with either of these two cases, under any interpretation of the excepted part (al-mustathna minhu) in this hadith.

* *

A point of view.

On examining this issue closely and stirring up dispute over it, it becomes apparent that the controversy and argument concerning it are greater than it can bear, and it is closer to being a matter of form than of substance. In practice it has no real existence.

The verification of this is as follows: As long as they agree on setting out for the Prophet's Mosque in order to greet the Messenger of God ﷺ, and they agree on greeting the Messenger of God ﷺ without fastening the saddles, then it will not be possible for a person to set out to greet him without going to the mosque, and this will not occur to anyone's mind. Likewise, setting out for prayer in the Prophet's Mosque without greeting the Messenger of God ﷺ will not occur to anyone's mind. Therefore, neither of the two is separable from the other, because the Prophet's Mosque is nothing but his house ﷺ. And is his house anything but a part of the mosque, as in the hadith of the Garden (al-Rawdah): "What lies between my house and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise"?

This is a strong link between his house and his pulpit in his mosque.

On another note: Does anyone greet him ﷺ from nearby, so as to obtain the merit of his returning the greeting, except when his greeting is from close by and from the mosque itself?

(p. 343) And would the visit be a Sunnah unless one enters the mosque and first performs the greeting prayer of the mosque (tahiyyat al-masjid)?

With this, there is no separation between setting out to the mosque and visiting the Messenger ﷺ, nor between visiting him ﷺ and the mosque. So there is no ground for this dispute.

Here is another point of view: his ﷺ saying: "No one greets me with peace except that God returns my soul to me, so that I return the greeting of peace to him." His statement, free of any condition of nearness or distance, indicates generality with regard to coming to greet him.

It is said: This is a great virtue, and it cannot be attained by one who is far away except by setting out to it, as a means to attaining it. And the means takes the ruling of the end, whether obligatory, recommended, or permissible. For example, walking to the Friday prayer is obligatory, because performing the Friday prayer is obligatory, and preparing fine clothing for it, for example, is recommended, because beautifying oneself for it is recommended. Likewise, preparing perfume for attending it.

I have seen Ibn Taymiyyah discuss this issue, but he gave examples that are open to debate. He said: Not every legitimate end has a legitimate means, such as a woman's Hajj and her going out to the mosque; for the first is conditional on the presence of a mahram (a close male relative she may not marry), and the second is conditional on the husband's permission.

The response to this is that a woman's travel in general is forbidden except with a mahram, whether it is for this mosque, for Hajj, or for something else.

And her going out to the mosque is not something required of her in principle, but if she requests permission, she is given it. So the default ruling in it is prohibition until she obtains permission.

On this basis, it is said: If setting out to it were not legitimate, then its doer would have no share in its virtue, and he would not obtain the return of the greeting from him ﷺ.

And if that were so, it would necessarily have been pointed out when stating its virtue, since delaying clarification is not permitted. For instance, one would say: "Then I return to him the greeting of peace, except one who sets out for that purpose," or one would say: "Whoever comes to me from nearby and greets me..." and so on. But nothing of this kind of pointing out has come, and the hadith remains in its generality.

Know that Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, distinguishes between greeting the Messenger of God ﷺ and greeting the Muslims in general, because the Messenger of God ﷺ has rights and distinctions that are not held by anyone else: the obligation of love, of reverence, the obligation of sending blessings upon him in our prayers, and greeting him when entering and leaving mosques, and indeed upon hearing his mention, which is never the case for anyone else.

(p. 344) Likewise, visiting others is for supplicating for them and asking God's mercy for them, whereas visiting him ﷺ and greeting him is so that God may return his soul to him, and he returns the greeting of peace to us.

And visiting anyone else, in any place in the world, has no particular merit, whereas visiting him ﷺ from his mosque has a unique status, and he has been granted what no one else has been granted.

I believe that this issue, had it not been for the disputes of Ibn Taymiyyah's contemporaries with him over other matters, would never have had any place or room for discussion.

But they found it sensitive and touching on emotion and love for the Messenger of God ﷺ, so they stirred it up and judged him to be holding a position that necessarily follows from his statement, namely: The saddles are not fastened merely for visiting; rather, they are fastened to the mosque for the sake of visiting, in accordance with the text of the hadith. Thus they attributed to him what he did not say explicitly. And if his statement were understood as a negation rather than a prohibition, it would be in agreement, i.e., such a thing would not be possible, because he did not forbid visiting the Prophet ﷺ or greeting him, but rather considered it among the virtues and acts of devotion. He only adheres to the text of the hadith in making the fastening of saddles directed to the mosque, and to everything, including greeting the Messenger of God ﷺ, as he stated clearly in his books.

He said in some of his epistles and responses, in the following words:

* *

A section.

I have mentioned in what I wrote on the rites (manasik) that travel to his mosque and visiting his grave, as the leading scholars of the Muslims mention in the rites of Hajj, is a righteous and recommended act.

I have also mentioned in several places in the rites of Hajj the Sunnah in this matter, and how one greets him, and whether one faces the chamber (al-hujrah) or the qiblah, according to two opinions. Most of them say one faces the chamber, like Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad, until he said:

Prayer is shortened on this recommended journey by the consensus of the leading scholars of the Muslims. None of the leading scholars (p. 345) of the Muslims has said that this journey does not permit shortening the prayer, nor has anyone prohibited travel to his mosque, even if the traveler to his mosque visits his grave ﷺ. Rather, this is among the best of righteous deeds, and there is nothing in my words or the words of others that prohibits it, nor any prohibition of what is legitimate in visiting the graves of the prophets and the righteous, nor of what is legitimate in visiting all graves.

He said further:

If visiting the graves of all believers is legitimate, then visiting the graves of the prophets and the righteous is more fitting.

But the Messenger of God ﷺ has a distinction that is not held by other prophets and righteous people, namely that he commanded us to send blessings upon him and greet him in every prayer, and this is emphasized in prayer, at the call to prayer, and in all other supplications; and that we send blessings and greet him upon entering the mosque, his mosque and other mosques, and upon leaving it. So everyone who enters his mosque must pray in it and greet him in the prayer.

Travel to his mosque is legitimate, but the scholars distinguished between it and other travel, when Malik, may God have mercy on him, disliked that one says: "I visited the grave of the Prophet ﷺ," because the legitimate purpose of visiting graves is to greet them with peace and supplicate for them, and that greeting and supplication have been achieved in the most complete manner in the prayer in his mosque and in other mosques, and upon hearing the call to prayer, and at every supplication. Thus sending blessings upon him is prescribed at every supplication, for he is more worthy of the believers than themselves. End quote.

If this is his statement, then the matter is one of form and not of substance. For he affirms that travel to his mosque ﷺ is legitimate even if one visits his grave ﷺ and greets him, and that this is among the best acts of devotion and righteous deeds.

That is, even if visiting is intended during the journey.

And if travel to the mosque is inseparable from greeting him ﷺ, and greeting him is inseparable from prayer in the mosque, then there is no ground for this debate, nor for making this matter a source of dispute or argument.

He has stated something close to this meaning in another place in his words, where he says, in vol. 27, p. 342 of al-Majmu' (Majmu' al-Fatawa), the following:

(p. 346) Whoever travels to the Sacred Mosque, or the Farthest Mosque, or the mosque of the Messenger ﷺ, and prays in his mosque and prays in the mosque of Quba, and visits the graves as the Sunnah of the Messenger of God ﷺ prescribes, then this is the one who has performed the righteous deed.

And whoever denies this travel is a disbeliever who is to be asked to repent; if he repents, well and good, otherwise he is to be put to death.

As for whoever intends travel merely to visit the grave, without intending to pray in the mosque, and travels to his city but does not pray in his mosque ﷺ nor greet him in the prayer, but goes to the grave and then returns, this is a misguided innovator, opposing the Sunnah of the Messenger of God ﷺ and the consensus of his Companions and the scholars of the Ummah.

This is the case in which two opinions are mentioned: one, that it is forbidden; the other, that there is nothing upon him and no reward for him.

What the scholars of the Muslims do is the legitimate visit: they pray in his mosque ﷺ and greet him upon entering the mosque and during the prayer, and this is legitimate by the consensus of the Muslims. He continued: And I mentioned that one greets the Prophet ﷺ and his two companions. End quote.

So what reason is there for dispute or disagreement over this statement? If his words about one who intends travel merely to visit the grave, without intending to pray in the mosque, and travels to his city but does not pray in his mosque ﷺ nor greet him in the prayer, but goes to the grave and then returns, "this is an innovator..." etc., were the basis of the dispute, then who among the Muslims permits a Muslim to fasten his saddle to Madinah merely to visit the grave without intending to pray in his mosque ﷺ, and without praying upon him ﷺ in the prayer, while knowing that prayer in his mosque ﷺ is worth a thousand prayers?

His words show that visiting the grave and praying in the mosque are linked, and whoever claims that they are separable in practice has opposed reality. When the link between them is established, disagreement is eliminated and the cause of dispute disappears. And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.

And in another place (p. 346), regarding the shortening of prayer during travel to visit the graves of the righteous, he stated four opinions from the companions of Ahmad. The third of them is: it is shortened for travel to the grave of our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

And in explaining this opinion he said: Since most Muslims must pray in his mosque, (p. 347) whoever travels to his noble grave has thereby traveled to his preferred mosque.

Similarly, some companions of al-Shafi'i said, and he continued: Likewise, many scholars use the term travel to his noble grave, and they hold that this includes travel to his mosque, since every Muslim who comes to the noble chamber must necessarily pray in his mosque; thus the two are inseparable in their view.

After quoting the scholars' opinions, he said the following:

The reality of the matter is that praying in his mosque is a necessary part of this journey. Everyone who travels to his noble grave must necessarily gain an act of obedience and nearness to God, for which he is rewarded by praying in his mosque.

As for the intention itself, the people of hadith intend to travel to his mosque, though some among them intend to travel to the grave as well, if they do not know the prohibition.

This is an extreme clarity from him that, in terms of reality, there is no separation between visiting and praying in the mosque according to the majority of scholars.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 72, verse 18 (part 6 of 7):

Then he said regarding the ignorant person: "As for one who does not know this, he may intend only to travel to the grave. Then he must pray in its mosque, and he will be rewarded for that. And what he does, while it is forbidden and he does not know that it is forbidden, will not be punished, so he obtains a reward and bears no sin." End of quote.

We have quoted extensively from him, because we found that many people are not aware of the matter, to the point that Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari* about it: "This is the gravest thing held against Ibn Taymiyyah." Although this is Ibn Hajar's testimony that it is the strongest criticism directed at him, along with what his opponents charged him with regarding creed and his fight against innovations, nonetheless, by God's grace, after these quotations from him, which are clear statements, nothing remains in them that could be considered grave. So everyone who speaks on this issue should refer to his statements, for he left no aspect unexplained, whether regarding the scholar or the ignorant person. And success is from God, the Exalted.

This is what relates specifically to travel to the Radiant City (Madinah) for the mosque and for visiting together, in the detail mentioned earlier.

As for the remaining places other than the three mosques, the saddles are not to be prepared (lit. "the riding beasts are not to be tightened") for them, whether for prayer, supplication, seclusion (i'tikaf), or the like, since no place has any distinction over another at all, whatever that spot or that act of worship may be (p. 348). This is based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah in the *Muwatta'* concerning the hour on Friday. He said: "I went out to Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and met Ka'b al-Ahbar, and I sat with him. He related to me from the Torah, and I related to him from the Messenger of God ﷺ. Among what I related to him was that I said to him: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'The best day on which the sun has risen is Friday. On it Adam was created, on it he was made to descend, on it he was forgiven, on it he died, and on it the Hour will take place. There is no creature but that it is attentive on Friday from the time the sun rises, out of fear of the Hour, except the jinn and mankind. And on it there is an hour in which no Muslim servant who is praying and asks God for something will encounter it without God giving him what he asked.'"

Ka'b said: "That is one day in every year." I said: "Rather, it is in every Friday." Then Ka'b read the Torah and said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ spoke the truth."

Abu Hurayrah said: "Then I met Basrah ibn Abi Basrah al-Ghifari, and he said: 'From where have you come?' I said: 'From Mount Sinai.' He said: 'If I had met you before you went out to it, you would not have gone. I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Riding beasts are not to be made to journey except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), this mosque of mine, and the mosque of Iliya' or Bayt al-Maqdis"'" Abu Hurayrah was unsure (which of the two).

Then I met Abdullah ibn Salam, and I told him about my sitting with Ka'b al-Ahbar and what I had related to him about Friday, up to the end of this great hadith.

Al-Baji said, commenting on this hadith: "Abu Hurayrah's going out to Mount Sinai may have been for a need that arose for him there, and it may have been that he intended it as an act of worship and drawing near to God by going there. However, Basrah's statement, 'If I had met you before you went out to it, you would not have gone,' is evidence that he understood from it that his intention was drawing near (to God). And Abu Hurayrah's silence when he was rebuked is evidence that what he understood was indeed his intention."

I say: Abu Hurayrah did state that it was for prayer, as in *Majma' al-Zawa'id* by Ahmad from Shahr, and he (al-Haythami) said: "Hasan" (good).

The hadith indicates that whoever vows to pray at the mosque of Basrah or Kufah should pray in his own place and not go to it, based on the explicit hadith of Basrah in this regard, since a vow only applies to what is an act of drawing near to God. There is no merit to the mosques of cities over one another such that it necessitates intending to journey to them by riding beasts, except the three mosques, for they are singled out for merit.

As for one who vows to pray and fast in one of the mosques of the frontier outposts (al-thughur), he is obligated to go there and fulfill his vow (p. 349), because his intention to go there was not for the sake of prayer in it, but was connected with garrison duty (ribat), and so fulfilling it is obligatory.

There is no disagreement about prohibiting this from any mosques other than the three, except what Muhammad ibn Maslamah stated in *al-Mabsut*. He added a fourth mosque to these, which is the mosque of Quba'. He said: "Whoever vows to go to it and pray in it must do so." End of quote.

Perhaps Muhammad ibn Maslamah's purpose in adding the mosque of Quba' was to act upon what came concerning the mosque of Quba' in a report specifically related to it from Anas ibn Malik, which Umar ibn Shabbah narrated. He said: Suwayd ibn Sa'id narrated to us, who said: Ayyub ibn Siyam narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn al-Ruqaysh al-Asadi, who said: "Anas ibn Malik came to us at the mosque of Quba', and he prayed two rak'ahs near some of these pillars. Then he gave the salam, and we sat around him. He said: 'Glory be to God! How great is the right of this mosque! Even if it were a month's journey away, it would be worthy of being visited. Whoever leaves his house intending it, purposely going to it to pray four rak'ahs in it, God will return him with the reward of an 'umrah.'"

The transmission of Wafa' al-Wafa' from it has already been mentioned, in his words: "This ruling was known among the common people, to the point that Ibn Shabbah said: Abu Ghassan said: 'What strengthens these reports and indicates their being widely known among both the common people and the elite is the statement of Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hakam in a poem of his:

"If I die, then I have gladdened an eye with the women who make the 'umrah to Quba',
Those whose necks are long and graceful, upon whom beauty is radiant."'"

A note.
The statement of Anas indicates the permissibility of undertaking a journey to Quba' even if it were far, but that is because of the merits of the other three mosques, so it does not contradict the first hadith.

Another note.
The poet's verses indicate the error of gathering on a specific day for Quba', and the mingling of men and women.

(p. 350) A third note.
There is a general difference in a summary manner between visiting graveyards in general for the common people, and visiting the graves of the three in particular. The purpose of visiting graveyards in general is to supplicate for their occupants and to remember the Hereafter, as he ﷺ said: "I had forbidden you from visiting graves; now visit them, for they remind one of the Hereafter."

As for these three honoured places, they have characteristics that no others share:

First: In terms of subject matter, they are connected to the Prophet's Mosque, one of the mosques for which riding beasts may rightly be undertaken.

Second: The great right that those within them have over the Muslims. By visiting them, one benefits not only by remembering the Hereafter, but also by recalling the memories of this world and the great struggle they undertook in the way of raising the word of God, supporting His religion, guiding the community, and upholding God's command, until God was worshipped alone and His law was put into practice. This stirs in the Muslim a feeling of the obligation to renew the covenant with God alone to act upon the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, and the guidance of his rightly-guided caliphs, may God be pleased with them.

This is what makes a person turn to God after greeting them with sincere supplication, that He may reward them for that with what He, glorified be He, knows they deserve.

Third: The great grace from God upon one who sends greetings to the Messenger of God ﷺ, that God returns his soul to him ﷺ so that he returns the greeting. All of that, or some of it, is not found at the graves in general. This is together with observing the legal etiquette of visitation, as previously mentioned.

* *

An issue.
In this noble verse: "And [We know] that the mosques belong to God, so do not invoke anyone alongside God" (Surah al-Jinn: 18), two matters are combined. The first seems to indicate the second by implication (mafhum), and the second is the explicit statement (manțuq) of the first, because the fact that mosques belong to God necessitates singling Him out for worship and that no one be invoked along with Him.

As for singling Him out for worship, the Shaykh, may God's mercy be upon us and upon him, wrote a complete discussion on this in Surah al-Hujurat, on a question arising from His statement: "O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds be nullified while you are unaware" (Surah al-Hujurat: 2).

(p. 351) In this issue he explained what is the right of God and what is the right of the Messenger of God, the obligation of singling out God, the Exalted, with what is His right, and he explained therein the etiquette of greeting the Messenger of God ﷺ, and that placing one hand upon the other in the manner of prayer is a form of worship that is not appropriate except to God, the Exalted. End of quote.

The combination here of the implicit and the explicit meaning, with the implicit meaning itself, indicates the intensity of concern with this matter and attention to its command. It draws attention to what came in the authentic hadiths of a strict prohibition and severe warning concerning the matter of mosques and the call to monotheism, and to what the early people used to do of building mosques over graves, thereby opening a door leading to polytheism. Such as the hadith of Umm Salamah and Umm Habibah, may God be pleased with them both, in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, in their account to the Messenger of God ﷺ of what they had witnessed in Abyssinia of this kind. He ﷺ said: "Those were people who, when a righteous man or a righteous servant among them died, built a mosque over his grave; those are the worst of creation in the sight of God on the Day of Resurrection."

And like the hadith in the two Sahihs: "God curses the Jews and the Christians who took the graves of their prophets as mosques." Aisha said: "Were it not for that, his grave would have been made conspicuous," meaning: out of fear that it would be taken as a mosque.

The hadith in the *Muwatta'* is his saying ﷺ: "O God, do not make my grave an idol that is worshipped. The wrath of God is intense upon a people who took the graves of their prophets as mosques." All of that emphasizes caution against combining graves and mosques, out of fear of temptation and as blocking the means (sadd al-dhari'ah) to it. This is supported by what the scholars of tafsir (may God have mercy on them) mentioned about the occasion of revelation: that the Jews and Christians, when they entered their churches and places of worship, associated others with God, so God warned the Muslims not to do that.

This issue is among those that have spread in many Islamic lands, which requires attention to it, and linking this verse to it together with those clear prophetic texts about it, whatever the mosque may be.

Ibn Kathir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "When this verse was revealed, there was no mosque on earth except the Sacred Mosque and the mosque of Iliya', Bayt al-Maqdis."

A note.
Some people have raised questions on this issue regarding the Prophet's Mosque and the location of the chamber within it after it was incorporated into it.

(p. 352) Ibn Hajar answered this in *Fath al-Bari*, in his comment on the hadith of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, that he ﷺ said during his final illness: "God curses the Jews and the Christians; they took the graves of their prophets as mosques." She said: "Were it not for that, his grave would have been made conspicuous, but I fear that it would be taken as a mosque." Narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Funerals.

In some of its narrations: "But he feared," and Ibn Hajar said: "Aisha said this before the Prophet's Mosque was expanded. For this reason, when the mosque was expanded, her chamber was made triangular and enclosed, so that no one could pray facing the direction of the grave while facing the qiblah." End of quote.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (*Adwa' al-Bayan*) on surah 72, verse 18 (part 7 of 7):

The books of biography (*sirah*) and the history of the Prophet's Mosque (al-Masjid al-Nabawi) mention some reports on this matter. Among them is what al-Samhudi narrates in *Wafa' al-Wafa'*. He said: And from al-Muttalib, who said: "They used to take dust from the grave. So 'Ā'ishah ordered a wall to be built against them, and there was a niche (*kuwwah*) in the wall, so she ordered the niche to be blocked up too."

It is also reported from Ibn Shabbah. Abu Ghassan ibn Yahya ibn 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Hamid said, and he was a scholar of the news of Madinah and from a family of scribes and learning: "The house of the Prophet ﷺ, in which he was buried together with Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, remained visible until 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz built over it the *khitar* (an enclosure) that is on it today, the *muzawwar* (the angled one), when he built the Mosque during the caliphate of al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik. He made it *muzawwar* only out of dislike that it should resemble the squaring of the Ka'bah and be taken as a *qiblah* toward which one prays."

Abu Zayd ibn Shabbah said: Abu Ghassan said: "I have heard more than one of the people of knowledge claim that 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz built the house other than its former construction. And I heard someone say: He built around the house of the Prophet ﷺ three walls, so below the grave there are three walls: the wall of the building of the house of the Prophet ﷺ, the wall of the house which he claims he built upon, meaning 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and the wall of the visible *khitar*."

He said: Abu Ghassan said, as related by al-Aqshahadi: "The trustworthy one informed me from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, from Mansur ibn Rabi'ah, from 'Uthman ibn 'Urwah, who said: 'Urwah said: I disputed with 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz concerning the grave of the Prophet ﷺ, that it should not be placed within the Mosque, with the strongest dispute. But he refused and said: The letter of the Commander of the Believers must be carried out."

He said: I said: "If it must be, then make for it a *ju'ju'*," that is, the place where we visit behind the chamber. End of quotation.

This, then, is a dispute concerning the chamber and the Mosque, and this is the answer of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, who came to the caliphate and was the fifth Rightly Guided Caliph. He confirmed this arrangement when those precautions were taken so that the grave would not become a *qiblah* for those praying. This is beyond doubt in the best generations, and in the presence of the great Muslims, which leaves no one room for objection, argument or proof. This question has been examined by the scholars of the Muslims in every age.

Al-Qurtubi said: The Muslims went to great lengths in blocking the means (*sadd al-dhari'ah*) concerning the grave of the Prophet ﷺ. They raised the walls around his tomb, blocked the entrance to it, and made it encircle his grave ﷺ. Then they feared that the place of his grave might be taken as a *qiblah* if it faced those praying, so that prayer toward it would take on the form of worship. So they built two walls from the two northern corners of the grave and angled them until they met at a triangular corner on the north side, so that no one could face his grave. End of quotation from *Fath al-Majid*.

Some scholars have said: This arrangement which was made in front of the noble grave and the graves of his two companions is in fact the answer to his supplication ﷺ: "O Allah, do not make my grave an idol that is worshipped," as Ibn al-Qayyim said in his *Nuniyyah*, as did Ibn Taymiyyah:

"The Lord of the worlds answered His prayer and surrounded it with three walls,
until its sides, by his supplication, were in might, protection and safeguarding."

The author of *Fath al-Majid* said: The hadith indicates that if the grave of the Prophet ﷺ were worshipped, it would be an idol. But Allah the Exalted protected it by placing a barrier between it and the people, so it cannot be reached.

The hadith also indicates that an idol is whatever the worshipper directly touches of graves and the coffins upon them. End of quotation.

What he has said is a truth whose basis is subtle, because if the chamber had not been brought within a safeguard against prayer toward it, it would have become an idol. Far be it from him ﷺ, who in his life called to Allah, that after he passed to the Highest Companion his grave should become an idol which contradicts monotheism and demolishes what he built during his life.

How could Allah be pleased with that for His Messenger? Far be it, indeed, no. This is the summary of what has been said on this question.

* *

(p. 354) A point of view.

Here is a point of view, though I have not come across a statement on it: every earlier text is explicit in prohibiting taking mosques over graves, namely that the grave comes first and then a mosque is built upon it, as came in the story of the People of the Cave: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said: "We will surely take over them a mosque"﴾. That is, the grave first and the mosque second.

As for the matter of the chamber and the Prophet's Mosque, it is the reverse of that, since the mosque came first and the inclusion of the chamber came second. So those texts do not, in my view, apply to it. And Allah knows best.

On another side: what was brought into the Mosque was not the grave or graves, but the chamber, that is, with what is in it. The words of the author of *Fath al-Majid* have already been cited in defining an idol: that it is what is prostrated toward from nearby.

On this basis, there is no one praying who is far from Makkah without there lying between him and the Ka'bah graves and cemeteries. Yet he is not considered as praying toward the graves, because of their distance and the barriers between. Even though the distance is relative. Likewise in the matter of the three graves in the chamber: they are far from direct facing in prayer toward them. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Also, Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, has a statement on this, summarised from *al-Majmu'*, volume 27, p. 323: "It seems that when the Prophet ﷺ died and was buried in the chamber of 'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and her chamber and the chambers of his wives were to the east and the south of the Mosque, none of that was within the Mosque. This continued until the era of the Companions in Madinah came to an end.

Then after that, in the caliphate of al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, about a year after his pledge of allegiance, the Mosque was enlarged, and the chamber was brought into it out of necessity. For al-Walid wrote to his deputy, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, that he should buy the chambers from their owners, the heirs of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, since they had all died, may Allah be pleased with them all. He ordered him to buy the chambers and add them to the Mosque, so he demolished them and brought them into the Mosque, but 'Ā'ishah's chamber remained as it was. It was closed, and no one was allowed to enter to the grave of the Prophet ﷺ, neither for prayer there, nor for supplication, nor for anything else, until the time when 'Ā'ishah was alive. She died more than twenty or thirty years before the chamber was brought in."

And he said on page 328: "She did not allow anyone to do anything at his grave of what he forbade (p. 355) and after her it was closed, until it was brought into the Mosque, its door was blocked up and another wall was built over it."

All of that is a safeguard for him ﷺ, lest his house be taken as a festival (*'id*) and his grave as an idol. Otherwise, it is known that the people of Madinah are all Muslims, and none comes there except a Muslim, and all of them revere the Messenger ﷺ. They did not do this so that the noble grave would be disparaged, but rather they did it so that it would not be taken as an idol that is worshipped, and so that his house would not be taken as a festival, and lest it be done to it as the People of the Book did with the graves of their prophets. End of quotation.

It has already been explained that Ibn al-Qayyim's account of the placing of the three walls and the making of the end of the third wall on the north side in the shape of the head of a triangle. Today, after Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim, the iron lattice (*shabak*) exists behind all of that. About six metres to the north of the apex of the triangle, at its centre, is a large prayer niche (*mihrab*), and this was in the Mosque previously, that is, before the lattice. This indicates the distance between the worshipper on the northern side of the noble chamber and the three graves, and negates any connection between praying behind it and the noble graves. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

At the end of this question, which has been raised with talk at the pilgrimage season of the year 1394 in Mina, and by some of those occupied with knowledge, we say:

If it had not actually been brought in, there would have been room for the claim that it should not be brought in. But since it has been brought in actually, and in the time of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and in the generations which are witnessed to be good, and thirteen centuries have passed since it was brought in, there is no room for that claim.

On another side: the Prophet ﷺ was silent about what is greater than that, namely the matter of the building of the Ka'bah, and that it did not include the foundations of Ibrahim, that it has one door, and that it is raised above the ground.

He ﷺ had the ability to rebuild it in the more correct form, so that it would include the foundations of Ibrahim, have two doors and level them with the ground. But he ﷺ left that, for considerations which he explained in the hadith of 'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.

Should not whoever speaks on the matter of the chambers today be content with what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was content with regarding the Ka'bah, and what the predecessors, may Allah have mercy on them, were content with regarding the chamber itself? (p. 356)

On a third side: if their view were adopted and it were taken out of the Mosque, that is, the Mosque were made to be without it, on the original basis.

Then others would come and say: "Let us restore it as it was in the time of the Rightly Guided Caliph 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz." Should not what Malik said to al-Rashid, may Allah have mercy on both of them, be said about the Ka'bah in particular, when Ibn al-Zubayr built it and al-Hajjaj rebuilt it, and al-Rashid wanted to restore it to Ibn al-Zubayr's construction? Malik said to him, may Allah have mercy on him: "Do not do it, for I fear that the Ka'bah will become a plaything of kings." So it can be said here too: the chamber will become a plaything of kings, between inclusion and removal. And in that is the trial that is in it. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

The author said, in (Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein﴾, the verse.

He used the singular pronoun in His saying "lahu" (for him) and used the plural in His saying "khālidīna" (abiding).

The answer is what has preceded: that the singular is according to the wording of "man" (whoever), and the plural is according to its meaning, and this is evident.
